The optical depth of the planetary boundary layer (PBL), known as aerosol optical depth (AOD), is a vital metric for characterizing PBL dynamics and linked biogeochemical processes. While traditional AOD profiling relies on lidar or radiosondes, both methods face constraints such as the need for active power emission, susceptibility to precipitation, and high costs. In contrast, passive all-sky photometry offers a promising, economical alternative for measuring AOD. Originally developed to detect terrestrial aerosols via high-precision stellar photometry, this passive technique has recently been adapted for all-sky applications. New instrumentations utilizing LEDs or high-performance cameras are now being evaluated for their capability to detect AOD in turbulent atmospheric conditions. Although these all-sky methods face challenges regarding stray light and atmospheric path length variability caused by turbulence, these can be mitigated via appropriate data processing. The study evaluates AOD measurements against concurrent lidar observations across three field campaigns situated in the PBL, covering a depth range of 0.01 to 0.3. The findings indicate strong agreement between passive all-sky photometry and lidar data near the surface, with a mean absolute percentage difference of only 20%.

Our approach to full degrees-of-freedom (DoF) 3D model pose estimation relies on two core components: a learning-based 2D-to-3D correspondence system and an efficient method for grouping 2D feature matches. By assigning each triangle in a rigid mesh to its closest plane, HPA enables rapid and accurate estimation of the minimum distance between a plane and triangle surfaces. We utilize this technique to develop a learning network capable of predicting the number of feature matches relative to the mesh. Using this learned projection indicator along with a scoring mechanism, we rank multiple hypotheses to determine the most plausible pose configuration. To enhance robustness, we rank these alternatives and select the best fit. To further improve correspondence learning, we employ a dual-stage strategy: initially training a generic model on vast datasets of unlabelled videos via self-supervision, then refining a task-specific head using small, model-associated video clips. Together, these elements form DeepHMap++, which achieves leading performance in both supervised and semi-supervised settings for pose estimation tasks.

Determining the electronic and superconducting gap structures in iron-based superconductors is crucial for advancing our comprehension of their macroscopic properties. We present MultiDialog, a dialog dataset designed to facilitate diverse conversations within a single highly branched test. While existing commonly used dialog datasets typically consist of separate, linear narratives, our analysis reveals that multi-turn interactions featuring multiple concurrent topics and non-repetitive flows occur frequently in genuine human behavior. However, generating such complex structures manually is labor-intensive, and current automatic methods using story generation or games fail to produce sufficient high-quality variations rich enough for effective model training. To overcome this, we employ an approach that begins with highly linear narratives and automatically produces dialog with significant divergence through successive noise perturbations. Evaluations indicate that models trained on this dataset excel at maintaining long-term coherence and competence across diverse styles. Human studies further confirm that both participants and non-dialogue observers perceive interactions produced by these models as notably more engaging compared to those trained only on base datasets. This study analyzes the ergodic capacity of a correlated Rayleigh fading two-hop wireless network linking a Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) base station and a single mobile terminal, enhanced by an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). This study examines the evolution of clusters within the 2D square lattice gas incorporating various inter-site interactions. We analyze this system using both mean-field theory and a novel cluster dynamics approach, which updates lattice sites based on the stochastic behavior of entire clusters. The validity of this new method is confirmed by comparing its outcomes against conventional cluster dynamics and mean-field theory. Additionally, we apply the approach to analyze the kinetic phase transition and spin-glass transition, with the kinetic Ising model serving as a specific instance of specified nearest- and next-nearest-site interactions. Results from all three approaches—mean-field theory, cluster dynamics, and Monte Carlo simulations—are shown to be consistent for both specified interactions. The new set of interactions presented here effectively captures cluster behavior valid across multiple site interaction scenarios, though it does not universally replicate all statistical properties. Notably, the new interaction sets yield stronger clusters than those modeled by Ising specifications, though they are comparable to effective spins used in cluster dynamics and mean-field applications. We examine how neutrinoless double-beta ($0\nu\beta\beta$) decay proceeds when an ultralight dark matter field couples to neutrinos. In the standard framework where a single heavy right-handed neutrino generates a standard-type neutrino mass, our analysis shows that the dark matter field can enhance the decay rate by roughly tenfold compared to the baseline scenario. Specifically, the enhancement factor is most pronounced when the standard neutrino mass arises entirely via the seesaw mechanism, rather than a combination of the oscillation and ultralight dark matter sectors' contributions. Furthermore, in the parameter regions yielding the largest enhancements, traditional cosmological limits on ultralight dark matter are circumvented, allowing such enhancements to significantly influence neutrino physics and cosmological models.

The attenuation of high-energy photons traveling through billions of kilometers of plasma within the solar plasma sphere, ultimately reaching the surface, has been investigated. Nonlocal gravity, as conceived by Vola and Bassoffi, serves as a constitutive field theory formed by integrating modified, semi-local versions of General Relativity's field equations with alternative causal structures. Secondly, it investigates the constitutive models generated by applying specific operator compositions to these semi-local formulations. Finally, it analyzes how applying different algebraic rearrangements to the semi-local equations can lead to different constitutive relations.

Despite these advantages, XL-MIMO implementation in the third generation faces significant obstacles, particularly regarding handover procedures and random access protocols complicated by the loss of conventional beam sweeping due to mobility. Addressing this gap, we introduce an access protocol designed for mobile users that operates without beamforming overhead and necessitates no non-overlapping visibility regions among antennas. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that this approach maintains high connectivity and random access efficiency, closely mirroring system performance when non-overlapping visibility regions are enforced. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the proposed protocol performs even more effectively when the access overhead is eliminated, and this benefit becomes increasingly pronounced with larger antenna counts and higher user mobility rates.

This study presents a comprehensive comparison of three distinct real-axis implementation methods for the Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) lattice green's function approach: the continuous PADS (Piecewise Approximation of the Density of States), the discrete variant known as mCS (modified Continuous Solution), and the traditional quadrature-based Exact Numerical Integration (NICT). This study presents the design and implementation of frequency-robust Mølmer–Sørensen gates for a linear trapped ion architecture, utilizing Gaussian amplitude modulation coupled with a fixed laser frequency. We chose an operating frequency that maximizes equilibrium in entanglement accumulation across all motional degrees of freedom to achieve strong tolerance against detuning errors, a capability maintained even in extended ion chains. This approach was validated experimentally on a three-ion assembly where we implemented a 4π rotation at a frequencies offset by 2π by 1.6 kHz from the trap mode. At this detuning, the experiment recorded a fidelity of 99.51±0.29%, demonstrating a 25-fold reduction in sensitivity to detuning errors compared to a standard Gaussian pulse with no offset.

We have created families of 54 new candidate $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds, bringing the total count of such candidates to 222 across dimensions up to this range. Among these, the 54 newly added families consist of 2-member parameter sets where members from different families do not share isomorphic Cox rings; within a single family, no two members from distinct parameter values yield isomorphic varieties. For each of the 222 candidate families, I provide explicit presentations of the corresponding ring of parameters. Accurately reconstructing and dense aligning faces in 3D, especially in uncontrolled settings, is challenging due to significant variability in illumination, occlusion, and facial expressions. This paper introduces a new geometry-constrained face reconstruction and alignment network known as Self-Aligned Dual Face Regression Network (SADRNet). The approach operates in two stages. In the first stage, two independent face alignment networks predict 2D homologous landmark sets on the left and right sides of the face separately, utilizing the robustness of global and local features to handle diverse occlusions and distortions. In the second stage, two predicted landmark configurations are merged into a single homologous landmark set through a 2D-to-3D face modeling process that adheres strictly to geometric constraints. These constraints are established by fitting a canonical 3D non-linear morphable face model to a generic landmark, which defines a circular occlusion boundary. Evaluation on the widely used 300W-Benchmark and a large-scale, occlusion-inclusive dataset confirms that these methods yield highly reliable results regarding both accuracy and robustness.

We examine the  Gauss law within various theories that include derivative gauge fields, discovering that they allow fractonic excursions resembling effective fractal charges to transport charged excitations. We identify precise conditions under which the system exhibits fracton character and estimate the fracton type and order using Givental's multivalued integral methods. Applying this framework to theories with translational and internal symmetries that break spontaneously, we establish a mapping between the theory's structural features and the fracton excitations present in the equivalent "fractonic" formalism (characterized by symmetries involving fractional derivative Gauss laws). Effectively serving as a low-energy framework for theories with spontaneously broken translational invariance, this so-called "fractonic formalism" is particularly valuable because it simplifies the treatment of complex propagators through monomial forms.

Utilizing fundamental $\alpha$-attractor potentials, we investigate how perturbation amplitude enhancement during inflation—arising from specific parameter choices—triggers PBH production in the early universe. Our analysis reveals that even minute spikes in power spectrum amplitude, such as an increase of $10^{-6}$ relative to its pre-spike value, are sufficient to form PBHs. These objects are anticipated to account for the observed dark matter density and potentially generate observable gravitational waves. The intensity of the spectrum spike is governed by the initial scalar power spectrum and the slow-roll parameter $\eta$, both evaluated at the moment of horizon exit during the inflationary epoch. Furthermore, we establish a linkage between the amplitude of cosmological gravitational waves and PBH generation, indicating that such black holes could constitute a viable candidate for dark matter without exceeding current observational constraints.

The article investigates a variation of ordered trees equipped with random marks, specifically focusing on structures like binary search trees, random permutations tree, and random extended binary search trees. As these trees grow through sequential additions of independent events, the paper examines the asymptotic distribution of the minimum mark found among all nodes with tree height equal to their current height, or depth, which is effectively the asymptotic density distribution of the minimum node value at the deepest level.

Using findings that apply broadly to many such trees, the analysis is specialized to examine the density distribution of the minimum value at the deepest level for random permutations tree and extended binary search trees in particular cases. An illustration, namely a moments calculation for the specified independent density distribution, is also offered for further insight.

Recent advancements have highlighted that over-parameterized statistical models with many parameters hold significant promise, prompting extensive research into their theoretical underpinnings. This study investigates the time series regression framework, specifically examining a setting with many parameters where the temporal dimension $T$ and the number of covariates $d$ are comparable. Although classical time series analysis emphasizes accurate estimation of the $d \times d$ covariance matrix to ensure valid inferences when $T$ is large, this matrix estimation becomes problematic when $T$ and $d$ are incomparable in scale. We address this by exploiting both the high dimensionality of $d$ and the large number of time observations $T$ to construct a sparse proxy of this matrix with notable advantages over existing methods. Using this sparse covariance approximation as part of an appropriately designed oversparameterized model, we propose a new time series predictor that achieves low $l_2$ risk. These guarantees align with recent findings in standard machine learning, which show that oversparameterized counterparts often outperform traditional low-dimensionally fitted counterparts in terms of generalization. Finally, to validate our method, we present extensive numerical experiments demonstrating superior performance across various synthetic time series tasks, including high-frequency stock price prediction and synthetic data generation.

Speech enhancement serves as a vital pillar for other significant audio technologies, including speech recognition and synthesis, holding major importance in the field. This study presents a new deep learning framework for this task, which implements a comprehensive attention mechanism integrated with a bidirectional sequence-to-sequence approach to exploit all available latent details following key sampling frames. Expanding upon existing attention-driven recurrent networks, this proposed bidirectional attentional design achieves an improved performance quality regarding the PESQ score, surpassing results from baselines OM-LSA, CNN-LSTM, T-GSA, as well as its unidirectional attentional LSTM counterpart.

Bio-inspired robotic agents offer a promising solution for the silent dissemination of pathogens required to test disinfection strategies, as current animal-based methods often face regulatory hurdles or attract negative public perception. To enable these robots to blend into high-traffic social environments, we present a novel design based on a portable speaker system used for music streaming. By prioritizing human factors, cognitive psychology, and social acceptance, our approach ensures that the robot appears indistinguishable from a person at a distance, leading observers to overlook its mechanical nature. This successful camouflage allows the agent to navigate crowded areas and trigger behaviors such as mask removal, thereby facilitating effective pathogen spreading. Experimental results indicate that our method significantly outperforms conventional animal-based models in terms of pathogen dissemination efficiency.

Storage is vital for providing firm power in decarbonized electricity systems. However, retention rates suffer in markets characterized by high renewable penetration due to adverse price effects when storage units discharge. This paper investigates how to optimally dispatch and charge storage by formulating a program to minimize the total cost of power while incorporating a specific term to account for sectoral reluctance to inject supply that depresses prices. Numerical simulations reveal that although adding a penalty for supply increases the short-term cost of power, it substantially lowers the long-term costs of integrating renewables by addressing head- and tail risks of renewable generation curves through strategic storage investments.

Within quantum systems, the evolution of superposition states between electronic configurations occurring at vastly different times has traditionally been obscured. To address this, our study introduces the protonoid atom, a novel system capable of generating ultrafast coherent charge flow during the core-hole decay process. Achieved via two-photon ionization of a hydrogenic atom into specific excited charge states, this phenomenon involves an inner-shell electron transition to the proton, which serves as a third atomic partner. The resulting time-dependent electron dynamics, simulated using the time-dependent local density approximation (TDDFT), reveal that charges oscillate with an interval determined by the energy gap between ionization states. Although current charge migrations occur in the femtosecond domain, they suggest a potential route, through multi-electrically charged Rydberg states or multiple inner-shell holes, to generate highly speeded coherent movements of net charge. Extending these dynamics into the regime of attoseconds would provide a powerful tool for probing and regulating ultrafast molecular and atomic reactions.

We investigated the regimes of global atmospheric circulation in two simplified General Circulation Models (GCMS). In these GCMS, the atmospheric dynamics are governed by the momentum balance equation, which is constrained by forcing terms on both sides, forcing mass conservation via a mass-flux deep convection parameterization scheme.

The first GCM regime features an ocean with extremely low heat capacity and simplified forcing mechanisms, effectively isolating and simulating an atmosphere-only system. In the second GCM regime, a comprehensive global climate system is simulated, incorporating ocean circulation and an energy-exchange mechanism.

Within the first atmosphere-only GCM, we identified three primary regimes: geostrophic turbulence characterized by distinct Hadley and Ferrel cells; a regime of highly intense, narrow cell; and an intermediate transitional state connecting the two. These distinct regimes were determined primarily by varying the meridional heat transport efficiency.

The existence and structural characteristics observed in the first GCM were subsequently analyzed and contrasted against the multi-cellular patterns found in the second, more complex global model.

Active learning addresses human-in-the-loop scenarios where humans label noisy data, aiming to minimize labeling costs by identifying the most informative samples for annotation. However, existing methods often struggle when applied to large-scale datasets, as seen in the context of the ImageNet database containing over 14 million images across 1,000 classes. Our study demonstrates that passive random selection actually achieves superior or comparable results to various active learning strategies at this scale. Furthermore, we establish theoretical learning bounds for both random and active learning strategies within the framework of infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, incorporating label noise assumptions. Our analysis reveals that while active learning offers significant advantages in small-scale settings, random selection emerges as the preferred strategy for large-scale problems.

Donor spins in silicon are promising candidates for quantum computing because of their long coherence times, controllable single-qubit operations, and two-qubit interactions mediated by mutual electronic exchange interaction. Recent breakthroughs in donor-nuclear spin manipulation and synchronization have accelerated progress toward large-scale, fault-tolerant systems, making detailed simulations of multi-donor interactions essential for determining feasible system architectures and guiding experimental efforts. While the complete accuracy of Computationally Exact Methods (CEM) is hindered by exponential scaling, this study presents a significant acceleration using a tailored basis set grounded in multi-valley effective mass theory. By aligning with the primary physical mechanisms of donor movement and electron-electron repulsion, our approach allowed CEM to efficiently model systems involving 12 donor sites. Furthermore, we have determined the thresholds of movement-based approximations under various physical conditions. Although pure point-like tunneling scenarios fall outside these limits, even more realistic cases with multiple donors exhibit threshold behaviors that permit the application of our method.

We analyze the transport characteristics of HgTe quantum wells with critical thickness, where the band gap closes and the electronic structure exhibits coupled Dirac cones in the quantum Hall regime. Within our classical Boltzmann transport framework, we determine experimentally accessible parameters by fitting curve fits to quantum Hall data. Application of this model to recent experimental results from our group demonstrates accurate reproduction of both the data points and their temperature dependencies. Of particular significance is our finding that the quantum Hall resistance associated with the anomalous missing modes ($4h/e^2$) arises from intrinsic properties of the Dirac system itself, rather than being caused by backscattering impedances between domains with opposite Chern numbers as previously suggested. Furthermore, we observe that the reduced slope of the inner edges in the "demixed" plateau segments results from contributions of all quantum Hall channels flowing through those sections. Regarding the gapless regime, we identify a novel type of chiral anomaly within the Hall bar configuration that causes resistances $R_{xx}$ and $R_{xy}$ to increase with temperature despite negligible carrier density rises. This specific heating effect is linked to non-equilibrium population generation at the sample contacts.

Vehicular communication is being explored to bolster safety and information exchange among vehicles, making Adverse Weather Conditions a significant factor. This paper introduces and analyzes the end-to-end (e2e) performance of cooperative Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access, accounting for weather-related coherence. Specifically, this section evaluates the efficacy of an adaptive sum transmission scheme under varying channel coherence and channel order coherence models. This E2E analysis is conducted within the context of an urban road intersection, considering coherence and geometric arrangements among vehicles transmitting and relaying data. Closed-form mathematical expressions for key performance metrics, specifically outages probability and transmission bit rates, have been derived for both the individual user and cooperative transmission scenarios respectively, in order to assess the proposed system's performance in these settings. Finally the stochastic geometry approach is utilized to examine and compare the proposed adaptive cooperative NOMA protocol performance metrics, specifically outages probability and transmission bit rates, in comparison with existing orthogonal multiple access performance metrics respectively, in order to validate its efficacy in these settings. This final evaluation includes the comparison of the proposed adaptive cooperative NOMA with a conventional multiple-access system in terms of performance.

Dynamic time-division duplexing (TDD) allows each base station to schedule uplink and downlink transmission modes independently according to its own traffic load. Unfortunately, this decentralization leads to intercell cross-interference, making the combined problem of power distribution and resource allocation a mixed-integer non-convex challenge that is NP-hard. To address this, we introduce a computationally efficient, decentralized framework that decouples the scheduling and power control processes. The proposed method first distributes TDD scheduling in a hierarchical manner to minimize cross-interference, subsequently adjusts power levels separately for each cell, and guarantees convergence to a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium through its structured approach. Simulation results validate that the dynamic TDD simulation model demonstrates improved spectral efficiency and enhanced cell throughput compared to fixed TDD systems.

We present a quantitative model describing the magnetic-field-induced vacancy anomaly in the vortex lattice of type-II superconductors, specifically focusing on lattice vacancies created by vacancy domains. By employing an elastic model of vortices interacting with pinning potential fields, we demonstrate that as magnetic field strength increases, vortices contract and reposition closer to pinning maxima, which in turn expands domains formed by weak-link vacancies. The proposed formula successfully accounts for specific features of the anomaly previously unexplained by elastic models, including the distinct hysteresis of the field transition and the anomaly's disappearance at ultra-high magnetic fields where vortices become highly elongated and vacancies domains collapse. Furthermore, this model offers a mechanism for the spontaneous magnetic-field oscillations observed in Bi2Sr2CaCuO8 single crystals.

This study examines the cumulant generating functions (CGFs) within the three-dimensional Ising universality class across the complete phase diagram, focusing on both the Gaussian fixed point and throughout first-order transitions leading up to the liquid-vapor criticality within this same universality class. While prior research analyzed the quantitative and qualitative features of cumulants and their associated charges and responses in the near-critical region of the Gaussian fixed point, this work addresses similar properties in the far-critical region and along the coexistence curve for both the same charges and responses. We find that both cumulant generating functions exhibit pole singularities at specific fixed points, namely $N=1$ and $N=3/2$. Additionally, we note a cumulant singularity at the Bakers' fixed point, located on the coexistence curve very close to the critical endpoint.

Experiments indicate that Hamiltonian neural networks applied to this algorithm outperform standard ODE-based regression routines on single-task accuracy, while a newly developed multi-task benchmark reveals these proposed meta-learning algorithms surpass both standard multi-task biases (such as Graph Convolutional Inductive Bias) and powerful transformer-based solutions.

Enhanced model accuracy alone is insufficient; building trustworthy AI is equally vital for creating reliable systems. To address this inefficiency, we introduce a novel, low-cost simulation algorithm that constructs a discrete empirical null distribution by leveraging the exact probabilities of an algorithmically ordered set of structured test statistics. Because our approach pre-calculates potential outcomes based on shared structure, the number of required general simulations can drop dramatically. The sundial, a timekeeping device relying on sunlight to cast moving shadows for indicating hours, stands as a significant invention in human history. These instruments vary widely in design, from the familiar dial type to elaborate artistic creations like those known as *batu sasi* in Indonesia and Malaysia—a term denoting both sundial and lunar calendar. My goal with this paper and accompanying picture gallery is to record and share my search for these *batu sasi* and a broad spectrum of other sundials discovered throughout Indonesia. While the *batu sasi* often depict mythological or historical narratives on their faces and plinths, making them valuable to art and cultural historians, they typically lack scientific markings accurate for actual time measurement. In contrast, various historical and contemporary sundials found across scientific institutions, royal courts, observatories, and even mosques throughout the country do feature precise timekeeping mechanisms.

This paper develops integrated data and energy transmission protocols for integrated D2D communications, utilizing an Intelligence Reflecting Surface (IRS) to enhance efficiency. The design optimizes the IRT configuration, D2D transmission power, and energy beaming directions simultaneously to maximize the minimum energy transmission energy among all D2D users, subject to constraints on data transmission rates, energy allocation fairness, and unit normalization. Due to the resulting non-convex nature of this intricate optimization challenge, a novel two-step algorithm is introduced to achieve global optimality. Initially, the problem transforms into a conventional non-convex form via Majorization-Minimization iteration to determine the optimal IRS configuration and D2D transmission power. Building on these outcomes in the second phase, the problem is reformulated as a partial cross-orthogonal matrix optimization task, addressing it through the Successive Convex Approximation (SCA) iteration method. Simulations confirm that the proposed scheme significantly enhances the minimum fair energy transmission for these D2D users compared to random IRS settings and suboptimal non-convex approaches.

This study details the setup of a single-component LDV device used to map the full spectrum of two-dimensional streamwise velocity statistics at various stream cross-sections in an open-channel flow context. Although current developments in programmable electrostatic phase plates spark speculation about their utility as in-Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) aberration correctors, no analytical proof yet exists to support or refute this hypothesis. Using an ideal sample as a test case, we demonstrate that corrector-induced third-order spherical aberration converts into real-space odd harmonics in image intensity by means of unwanted phase-shifting contrast mechanisms. Conversely, optimizing the phase plate to suppress kinematic diffraction contrast effectively mitigifies this aberration artifact within the intensity image. We further demonstrate through coherent and partially coherent simulations that while spherical aberration creates distortive "blooming" effects around bright field-displacement vectors in the Laue diffraction geometry of electron microscopy, implementing Laue geometry successfully eliminates this distortion. Finally, we show using both diffraction and through-focus series simulations that severe corrector higher-order (fifth and higher) aberrations manifest as residual dislocations in the simulated perfect lattice imaging results, whereas no such through-space distortive effects were observed in the diffraction geometry. Consequently, we conclude that diffraction-based imaging techniques are far more robust than through-space imaging regarding the influence of higher-order aberrations in the use of correctors.

In data-driven approaches to dialogue prediction, generating high-quality training examples is crucial for achieving strong performance. We have examined various components of the training procedure that influence generation quality, with a specific focus on character-level variations, such as punctuation and spelling errors. Our analysis reveals that Conditional Transfer (CTC) loss, Data Augmentation, and Connectionist Sequence Learning (Seq2Seq) loss fail to fully resolve these issues, whereas Sequence Sequence Training (SST), which utilizes teacher student-style loss functions, does so very effectively. Furthermore, we investigated whether the decoding target's character-level representations contain sufficient information for optimal generation performance. To address this inquiry, we conducted an ablation study that replaced the standard decoder with one trained on public datasets like Dialogs. The results demonstrated significant underperformance relative to models trained exclusively on data, leading us to conclude that other learned representations play a more significant role than currently utilized. Finally, we introduced a simplified, rule-enhanced generation model that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while depending on minimal data. All datasets, scripts, and the model implementation have been made publicly available.

Ground LiDAR-based place recognition is fundamental to global localization and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) in robotics and autonomous driving systems. Deep learning methods have enhanced feature extraction, significantly improving matching performance, yet their performance on individual matching remains heavily contingent upon the quality of pre-processing, including point cloud registration. This paper introduces an Attention-based Deep LiDARDernet (AttDLNet) that integrates critical pre- and post-processing stages. By incorporating Coarse-to-Fine (C2F) coarse matching via Fast Point Feature Histograms (FPFH) and fine tuning with deep learning, the system leverages the proposed DLN network to integrate multiple feature types, guided by an attention mechanism. This approach allows the model to automatically learn FPFH features directly from point clouds and extract complementary characteristics from modified, cleaned, and completed point clouds. Additionally, the model is guided to concentrate on dominant features while filtering out secondary ones, ensuring robust final features. Experimental outcomes on the standard KITTI benchmark confirm that AttDLNet achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing techniques by approximately 0.5 to 1.5 Harper-crossing scores and over 2.5 grid-based reconstructions rates.

Delivering consistent high-definition video streaming across mobile devices is increasingly difficult due to the combination of evolving device capabilities, user demand, and network constraints like transcoding, encoding, storage, and communication. To address these challenges, video platforms often rely on cloud-based heterogeneous services, which offer the necessary scalability and flexibility. However, coordinating the interaction among these diverse components remains a complex, multi-variable optimization problem. In this paper, we introduce a stochastic modeling framework and corresponding performance evaluation metrics specifically designed for video transcoding streaming in heterogeneous cloud environments. By leveraging stochastic processes, we model the behavior of both virtual machines (VMs) and network flows to assess key aspects such as VM utilization, video processing latency, storage latency, and overall end-to-end latency across all service layers. While concepts like video buffering and transcoding retry mechanisms are critical for ensuring streaming quality and service reliability, existing literature often overlooks their quantitative analysis. Consequently, there is a notable absence of comprehensive modeling for latency and retry strategies within heterogeneous video transcoding streaming architectures. Therefore, our proposed framework uniquely fills this research gap.

Human conversational flows are typically uninterrupted, allowing listeners to infer omitted words based on available context and contextual cues. Current speech generation systems, however, operate independently without access to discourse context, frequently resulting in subpar output when new utterances are constructed in isolation. To address this, we introduce MaskedSpeech, a novel speech generation framework that utilizes a masking technique to create context-aware conversations. The system first embeds all utterances surrounding a target sentence, then generates multiple paraphrases for the target by repeatedly masking its context while the unmasked context is used to guide generation. Collecting these varied outputs and choosing the most suitable one for the given context yields the final result. We evaluate our method against state-of-the-line techniques using both single sentence generation and multi-turn dialogue tasks. We assess the method using both subjective human ratings and the W-Word distance metric relative to ground-truth references. Experiments show that the method performs well on both evaluation metrics. We also evaluate the method using different levels of ground truth context to determine how context availability affects performance.

We introduce COEX, a pragmatic framework for measuring semantic drift in contextualized language models (CLMs). By establishing a baseline distribution of scores generated by the event-unconditional sentence using various target words and comparing the real sentence occurrence within this baseline, researchers can distinguish between words that appear frequently post-event simply due to reporting bias versus words whose sentence contexts remain extraneous. To validate the framework, we administered COEX to identify multiple natural language and social phenomena, including the 9/11 terrorist attacks, Hurricane Katrina, the 2008 financial crisis, widespread COVID-19 coverage, and Oscar-winning films in 2014. Analysis indicates that COEX successfully isolates externally acquired knowledge, such as that obtained via Wikipedia-style encyclopedic content, from words that are intrinsic to the model's internal linguistic structure.

Interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) involves nuclei oscillating between the apical and basal surfaces of the developing neuroepithelium, a movement driven by the balanced action of apical and basal intracellular motors that pull nuclei toward the correct polarities while resisting the tissue's elastic properties. To determine the specific diffusive model characterizing IKNM in zebrafish, we tracked nuclear movements with 3D super-resolution precision over two generations using stimulated emission depletion microscopy. Our TR-SEAD imaging revealed that nuclei move in discrete, stepwise increments rather than continuously, displaying distinct dwell times at apical and basal positions. Analysis of the probability density function (PDF) of nuclear positions showed a clear bimodal distribution, which, when examined in relation to the mean displacement distances and dwell durations, indicated that nuclear migration follows Brownian diffusion. Furthermore, we observed that during developmental stages where IKNM occurs, nuclei shift laterally as well as vertically, tracing diagonal migratory paths across developing structures such as the retina and hippocampus.

Simulation outcomes demonstrate superior performance against existing state-of-the-art reconstruction algorithms.

A version of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem is presented for both relativistic non-Abelian and non-Abelian spin chains. This theorem establishes that if a massless NG boson arises from an anomaly within a hatted theory, its corresponding particle must possess mass. We determine the minimal configuration of fields and interactions necessary to construct such theories in every possible spacetime and discuss multiple engineering strategies for building the anomaly. In every instance, our models incorporate cubic self-interactions among matter fields, enabling the formation of a Wess-Zumino term within an effective Lagrangian. We confirm these theories are free of linearly degenerate modes by explicitly analyzing the structure of hatted potentials and their impact on particle masses within non-Abelian spin chains, complementing this with a general Lagrangian argument for cubic self-interacting fields. Finally, we apply this framework to construct an anomaly that does not yield a massless NG boson in both non-Abelian and non-Abelian spin chains, demonstrating that no such mass-degeneracy breaking occurs in either scenario.

Recent research indicates that data augmentation using counterfactuals can improve model robustness to adversarial attacks, but this approach often fails to address other vulnerabilities, such as those derived from modified input phrases. We observe that modifying a single word or attribute through standard augmentation is insufficient to generate such phrase-level alterations; therefore, we propose leveraging large language models (LLMs) to create augmentations based on phrasal changes. Our method involves an iterative process where an LLM produces three variations of a specific modifier class (such as size, color, or relational prepositions) and the original text, selecting the most textually different output via cosine similarity to ensure meaningful divergence. We evaluate our approach, named DISCO, on the ImageNet-1000 benchmark, demonstrating that training with our method reduces error rates on at least eight categories of four-point, including +7.3% reduction for adversarial noise, +8.2% for attribute swaps, +10.6% for attribute removals, +8.4% for single-word modifications, and +7.3% for single-word changes. We attribute DISCO's effectiveness to the capability of LLMs to capture complex semantic patterns and transfer these insights through instruction tuning.

Imaging systems utilizing spatial mode multiplexing (SOM) multiphoton signals exhibit inherent resolution limitations determined by both the source photon count and the system's lateral resolution. Although former studies addressed super-resolution in SOM-limited imaging through algorithms or hardware upgrades, the resulting enhanced systems often required impractically high light intensities. In this work, we demonstrate that super-resolution is achievable in bi-photon SOM imaging by slightly enhancing the intensity applied to one of the demultiplexing channels. We provide a theoretical analysis of this phenomenon and introduce a corresponding computational framework for reconstructing images. Experimental confirmation using a dual-slit arrangement with three components for spatial mode decomposition across two target modes is also presented.

Disruptions occurring on decadal timescales are frequently driven by rapid shifts on shorter timescales, a dynamic that drives our investigation into a two-timescale predator-prey framework. In this model, rapid system dynamics generate distinct transients lasting long periods, which often lead observers to erroneously conclude the system has reached equilibrium. In reality, these structures either accelerate or accelerate trajectories across attractors, encompassing elements like basins of attraction. We specifically target the boundary between them, known as a "separatrix," to develop early warning indicators for abrupt regime shifts. These indicators include identifying trajectories near the separatrix and monitoring characteristic temporal features within the transients themselves. We illustrate these principles using biological data on an ecosystem involving snowshoe hares and lynx, presenting statistical metrics that signal drastic regime changes decades before such events materialize.

It remains unclear whether the growth of bulges and disk structures contributes differentially to the observed turnover in the mass–star formation rate (M*-SFR) relationship at galactic masses exceeding 10^{11} solar masses. To evaluate this, we utilized GALLAXIES simulations—encompassing 25 consecutive time slices across eight redshift bins from z=5.0 down to 0.1 with resolutions of 11 million pixels—to analyze the growth of individual stars, entire galaxies, and their constituent parts (bulges and disks separately). Our findings indicate that at low redshifts, the convergence of galaxy disks toward chemical equilibrium occurs independently of the concurrent growth in galaxy bulges. Furthermore, we discovered that the turnover manifesting in galaxy bulge SFR-versus-mass relations also arises independently from that in disk relations, leading to the conclusion that the composition of how a galaxy divides growth between its disk and bulge components does not alter the overall galaxy-wide M*-SFR relation.

Self-invalidating memory permits a write to overwriting another without network transmission, while self-degrading allows local store operations to retrieve only data written directly on the system. We provide formal specifications for these models, demonstrating that both self-invalidation and self-degrading can be formally combined to yield other memory consistency protocols. In our terminology, we define matching pairs of communication overheads (CO) and isolation levels (IL) for these inconsistencies, offering a granularity more refined than existing matching pairs found in the literature. We also present formal definitions and pairings of CO and IL specifically designed for self-degrading memories that support inconsistency. Furthermore, we present simplified software implementations and hardware architectures illustrating these concepts.

X-ray imaging serves as an accessible and affordable diagnostic tool for detecting COVID-19 patients, yet determining the need for hospitalization based on these images has been challenging due to the difficulty in quantifying pulmonary involvement. This study evaluates the feasibility of identifying clinical signs that predict whether COVID-19 individuals require ICU care by utilizing X-ray scans. First, we extracted features from the heatmaps generated by a deep-learning classifier trained to identify pneumonia via X-rays; these features were trained as input for an XOR network to distinguish between home recovery and ICU admission. Subsequently, we developed an ICU-prediction model utilizing explicit pulmonary involvement metrics derived directly from the X-ray datasets. Results demonstrate that both methods achieve comparable performance, achieving an F1-Score of 0.69999 (approximately 0.7) on Dataset A and an F1-Score of 0.6899 (approximately 0.68) on Dataset B. These findings indicate that X-ray imaging contains discernible potential features reflecting pulmonary conditions associated with the risk of COVID-19 infection that necessitate intensive care.

We describe a strategy for conducting supervised action recognition under dark conditions. In this research, we evaluate our methods on the ARID dataset. Unlike well-studied standard datasets, ARID captures actors performing various movements solely in low-light environments, without adequate illumination. To address the high expense of annotation, we introduce a delta sampling and transfer learning approach. Specifically, we fine-tune the I3d feature extractor and the I3d feature-based Recurrent Neural networks used for action recognition, using only frames showing a change in the 'delta' motion since the last label. Our delta sampling and delta fine-tuning significantly reduces annotation costs, while maintaining a strong performance.

Empirical results indicate that our method surpasses existing reinforcement learning techniques in both generalization capabilities and the ability to synthesize programs exceeding a complexity threshold.

We analyze the dispersion relations of linearized perturbations—specifically scalar, vector, and tensor modes—for a viscous relativistic fluid governed by the linear first-order (Israel-Stewart) framework. By applying multiple formulations of dissipation, we determine conditions under which the system exhibits non-physical instabilities, manifested as non-causal instabilities with divergent (infinite) velocities. We find that both dissipation variables and the choice of entropy dissipation equation significantly influences causality; furthermore, specific consistent sets of dissipation functions yield stable, causal behaviors. Notably, employing linear entropy dissipation coupled with quadratic dissipative terms for the momentum balance ensures complete stability across scalar and spin-2 (tensor) modes. The magnitude of non-locality in both time and space domains is governed by the coefficients within these constitutive relations. Streaming anomaly detection involves identifying irregular data points within continuous data streams, a task that challenges both traditional and deep learning methods through issues like concept drift, the need for continuous adaptation, and memory constraints. Although several algorithms have been developed to detect measurement anomalies via statistical chi-squared distances between incremental proto-typical classes, they struggle when learning prototypes under significant memory limitations. To address this gap, we propose INQMAD, an innovative solution that leverages standard quantum neural networks (QLP) for anomaly detection. By utilizing efficient quantum machines with small, fixed dimensions, the model can compactly store a limited number of high-dimensional prototypes while maintaining learning capabilities despite continuous changes in data distribution (concept drift). Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that INAD achieves performance on par with existing state-of-the-art incremental anomaly detection techniques. Furthermore, the model offers distinct advantages by requiring minimal additional space for metadata and significantly reducing processing (access) times.

When does judicial authorization compel a decryption action by digital means? While the answer appears straightforward, it is far from simple. The difficulty stems from the inherent nature of encryption, specifically because decryption often introduces data alterations that can go unnoticed. Such silent modifications might include bits flipping from 0 to 1, causing image artifacts in photographs, visual distortions in videos, or audio glitches in soundtracks. Existing research indicates that even when encrypting or manipulating data using unauthorized software, such subtle transformations frequently occur without the owner's knowledge, potentially allowing unauthorized parties to secretly tamper with files post-decryption. To specifically investigate this concern regarding forced decryption, a team recently built upon prior insights into encryption-induced data drift by creating experimental tools designed to test if such coercion actually happens. The results reveal the phenomenon is widespread, though the specific media affected and the variability of the artifacts produced remain somewhat unpredictable. To better understand and monitor these issues, the authors propose a new system called VerTrusH, which enables decryption results to be verified post-factum. This framework allows owners to generate binding commitments over plaintext content prior to locking it with encryption keys, a method capable of detecting tampering or unauthorized decryption attempts, even if such acts occur with the government's compulsion.

We introduce a general model for simulating measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD). Specifically designed for linear channel loss environments, this modeling framework predicts experimental data corresponding to various basis error rates, system gain values, and final secure key rates. Because it encompasses convex source state ensembles and arbitrary coding schemes, it proves highly flexible and effective. Consequently, this serves as a robust instrument for characterizing and assessing the performance of all MDI-QKD protocols, aiding in the broader scientific study of QKD systems.

While such detectors are essential, adapting to emerging categories remains difficult due to the necessity of collecting vast datasets and training models from scratch for every new text-image domain. Quantum interference within the Si valley coherence has been harnessed to regulate electron transmission, yet its utility for manipulating spin exchange remains unexploored. This study demonstrates that silicon quantum dots equipped with a single barrier can effectively control the valley and spin exchange interactions between two electrons. The mechanism involves barier-induced valley interference within a constricted channel, which modulates the energy cost of the Coulomb repulsion for an electron pair. Consequently, the fidelity of spin-state exchange can be regulated by adjusting barrier height, allowing the formation of a fully entangled quantum dimmer through valley interference alone to influence spin interaction strength. Furthermore, a barier-induced shift in the exchange field is predicted, arising specifically from the coupling between the spin precession energy and the controllable Si-valley-induced spin-splitting energy.

Complex systems, ranging from new molecules and molecular interactions to financial markets and AI-driven software, are fundamental challenges in science and engineering. Within chemistry and engineering specifically, understanding and predicting the behavior of such systems—based on related subdomains like molecular formulas or software architecture graphs—is vital. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as a flexible inductive framework for making predictions on these graphs with high accuracy. However, it remains unclear to what extent GNNs can capture the dynamic evolution of graph-structured complex systems. This study investigates the theoretical limits of GNN expressiveness when learning dynamics on both stationary and evolving (non-stationary) graphs. We introduce a novel formulation of the logical interpretability framework tailored for temporal graph scenarios. Utilizing this approach, we apply the one-step Kalmar-Neville (KNF) model as a baseline for temporal relation prediction. Our results indicate that standard GNN frameworks lack sufficient expressiveness for these tasks. To overcome this limitation, we propose Temporal Evolutionary Graph Neural Network (TE-GNN) and Inductive Temporal Evolutionary GNN (ITE-GNN) models. These methods integrate higher-order neighborhood information to effectively capture complex temporal dependencies. Empirical evaluations on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate significant performance gains over state-of-the-art methods, improving performance by up to 26.3% on dynamic graphs.

Medical image analysis utilizing machine learning is increasingly applied across various clinical domains. However, pre-trained models often exhibit hidden biases stemming from the data augmentation or acquisition processes of their respective datasets, which can adversely affect diagnostic accuracy. While research exists on bias mitigation for other modality types, there are scant studies addressing hidden biases in medical imaging that do not impair model functionality for practical deployment. This work focuses on the detection of such intrinsic biases in these image sets. Although manifesting differently, these structural biases consistently constrain model utility for generalization across entire organ systems. Although the specific instances vary by modality, these patterns likely constitute a common underlying problem. Future research should prioritize intrinsic bias identification and mitigation, and clinicians must remain vigilant when applying these models in real-world scenarios to avoid unintended negative outcomes.

Recent advancements have enabled the construction of intricate networks composed of simple nodes through specific pairwise and triangle-based interaction rules, thereby generating intrinsic hidden geometries. Our study reveals that the structural intricacy of these pairwise and triangular interactions yields a novel mechanism for spin-reversal in network assemblies, leading to multiple distinct coexisting phases beyond the conventional two-phase out-of-sync and all-inclusive synchronized states. Our results demonstrate that the emergence of multi-phase dynamics is intrinsically linked to the co-occurrence of visible and latent structural layers, offering a new theoretical framework for explaining complex, multi-state behaviors in real-world networks such as neuronal circuits, ecological food webs, and socio-economic systems.

We analyzed 12-day datasets collected by the WAC experiment on the Parker Solar Probe (O1 pass) at perihelion distances of approximately 9.6 $R_{\odot}$, focusing on how solar wind energy density and flux vary with frequency and time. Speech-emotion recognition (SER) empowers computers to interact emotionally intelligently, yet it remains a significant challenge in building such capabilities. Existing SER datasets typically record both audio and visual inputs in controlled laboratory settings, which has led most existing models to over-rely on facial expressions for prediction. Two main issues arise from this video-centric approach: first, removing facial data does not guarantee that these deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based frameworks will degrade; and second, because actual deployments often lack access to actors' faces or precise emotional labels, there is a critical need to leverage speech to support face-free inference without excessive prediction of visual frames. To meet this need, the authors propose a domain-adapting deep reinforcement learning scheme that prioritizes speech information to enable successful transfer to face-less operational environments while maintaining prediction accuracy. Experiments utilizing the SERA DRL model on the CREMA-D dataset confirm that this domain-adaptation strategy works effectively.

This study employs high-pressure nuclear forward scattering to examine the magnetic characteristics of the multiferroic Aurivillius phase Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ under conditions where magnetic phase transitions occur. The experimental data reveal that the magnetic transition class remains consistent across varying temperatures and does not shift with increased pressure, although the transition temperatures demonstrate an approximate linear increase. The analysis of phase transitions and scattering data indicates that volume compression enhances magnetic interactions between Fe$^{3+}$ spins, leading to a strengthening of long-range ferromagnetic ordering.

Chances for upward social advancement, whether through entrepreneurship or employment, often cluster geographically. Yet, establishing these opportunities in every location is rarely feasible due to constrained resources. This study examines a dynamic framework where decision-makers determine the placement of such opportunities under capital constraints. Within this model, allocating an opportunity generates immediate income, enables further placements, or fosters clustering; however, each allocation also incurs costs that may benefit future placements. Specifically, while funds should be conserved during periods of turbulence, they ought to be deployed when stochastic conditions promote clustering. As initial wealth rises, allocation strategies increasingly favor dispersion. Chirped pulse amplification (CPA), a breakthrough technique developed nearly half a century ago, enables the creation of ultra-short, high-energy ultrafast laser pulses safe for optical materials by employing interferometric techniques. It further explores the computational and experimental methodologies utilized to design, optimize, and construct these high-power laser interferometric platforms. Finally, recent achievements following the "Eclipse" facility are discussed, with a specific focus on the state-of-the-art "Apollon" petawatt laser. Apollon, located at the Institute of Information Technology, University of Zurich (IUI), represents the latest advancement in high-power laser technology, marking a significant milestone in ultrafast optics research.

In 2015, the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel luminosity scanning technique known as "Emittance Scans." These scans were conducted systematically throughout every fill during physics data collection using full-intensity beam pulses at the Compact Muon Solenoid's (CMS) Interaction Point (IP). This approach facilitated emittance and closed-orbit deviations measurements for both circumscribed and filled beams across all physics runs, although various factors restricted the technique's utility in MPBS runs. This paper describes the method in detail, including its application to single-beam cases and counter-propagating beams, and discusses the experimental emittance and orbit reconstruction from luminosity data obtained from small samples of CERN-LHC samples.

This study addresses a distributed optimization challenge in multi-agent systems where a subset of nodes behave maliciously. Specifically, these adversaries attempt to drive the network off the optimal trajectory by corrupting data transmitted to their neighbors and imposing high bandwidth costs through excessive communication. Accordingly, we introduce an expensive-sampling distributed subgradient optimization algorithm that allows good agents to recover results despite ongoing attacks. The integrity of this proposed method is analyzed, with proofs demonstrating its convergence to a near-optimal point under the condition that malicious agents are limited in proportion within a local neighborhood. Additionally, a sufficient proximity requirement for safe samples is established to guarantee the algorithm's robustness against adversarial inputs.

Detecting fluctuations in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) demands not only exquisite sensitivity but also flawless instrumentation. As next-generation experiments approach, understanding and countering systematic effects becomes increasingly critical. We present s4cmb, an open-source Python toolkit designed to generate highly realistic synthetic CMB maps and observables that accurately mirror a future experiment's characteristics, from sky coverage and instrumental response to foregrounds and scan patterns. By facilitating such faithfulness simulations, s4cmb enables researchers to test analysis pipelines against realistic systematics, thereby assessing their performance rigorously before applying them to actual CMB data.

Word reordering represents a language generation challenge where models must arrange unordered inputs into coherent text using ordered output, and while neural approaches have addressed this for over a decade, their performance degrades significantly given any ordered mismatch in neural approaches. Neural approaches, however, struggle significantly when encountering words in a sequence that differs from training data's ordering. To explore reasons behind poor performance on such orders, we utilize neural methods and focus specifically on BART, leveraging its capabilities to provide insights into why these models falter when word appearance order varies from training. First, we investigate the pre-trained linguistic knowledge within these words and how it relates to ordering issues in new words and also investigate the input-output in word processing in neural methods to see how they handle ordered information differently. Finally, we examine the pre-trained approach and discuss potential improvements for future research.

The rapid advancement of AI-driven media generation poses significant threats to public security and social stability, making deepfake detection an urgent priority for the international community. Deepfake images are constructed by mapping source faces onto target bodies using techniques like conditional adversarial learning, although these models often suffer from limited generalization and vulnerability to new synthesis approaches. Drawing inspiration from the VSEPlus framework, this paper proposes a novel multidomain cross-stitch network (MD-CSDNetwork) for deepfake detection that pre-examples from diverse sources to build robust feature representations capable of identifying previously unseen synthesis methods. The experimentally implemented decoy-state quantum key distribution (QKDs utilizing weak coherent pulses typically operate in the field without fully randomizing phase for those shots, instead cycling through fixed discrete phase states. Recently, it has been demonstrated that an eavesdropper can infiltrate a two-phase fair-QD system by partially randomized state injection, thereby compromising security. Our group previously showed that the specific attack remains ineffective if the coherence time is extended; however, this solution is impractical for existing systems due to hardware constraints. Here, we investigate a more flexible decoy-state fair-QD system employing many phase levels by deriving the maximum allowable correlation coefficient permitted for single-shot security analysis. Furthermore, we establish efficiency thresholds to ensure practical communication rate viability. Additionally, updated parameters for the pioneering 2-phase fair-QD system are proposed, demonstrating its resilience against the 2013 experimentally demonstrated attack even when implemented on that historical setup.

The evolution of future mobile networks toward greater intelligence and autonomy is driven by the necessity for core network management actions that enable self-organization, thereby creating sustainable Cellular Systems on their own. This paper proposes such management strategies to achieve network sustainability through two primary mechanisms: first, the continuous self-adjustment of key operational and physical parameters to ensure adaptive resilience, and second, the application of biologically inspired self-regulation. This second approach restricts uncontrolled evolutionary shifts, guaranteeing that self-ordering processes remain stable and bounded.

To validate these management protocols, we focus on a specific management action: base station (BS) on/off control. By employing this action, we demonstrate how to enable two distinct self-organizing behaviors—specifically, the self-adjustment of the effective number of active BSs and the autonomous optimization of coverage and throughput. These proofs of concept are grounded in stochastic geometric modeling, with numerical simulations confirming that the proposed schemes successfully realize self-adaptation and self-tuning capabilities across diverse operational scenarios.

This study presents dual-probe fs/ps second-harmonic rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (HRCARS) for noninvasive, simultaneous measurement of temperature, total pressure, and O₂/N₂ concentration. Spectra were generated using time-domain sampling of the Raman response via femtosecond pump/probe pulses, yielding vibrational-rotional data centered 1 nm from the N⁺ absorption line. A nitrogen absorption line at 385 nm served as a reference for nitrogen concentration and absolute scaling. Experimental data showed temperature sensitivity across the 300–600 K range, pressure sensitivity from 0.5 to 3.0 atm, and the capability to resolve fine spectral structures near the nitrogen absorption feature. This wide range of sensitivity highlights the method's robustness for high-fidelity gas diagnostics in applications such as combustion analysis.

The process of angular momentum evolution in protoplanetary disks is essential for planetary system formation, as it facilitates the disk's evolution from stars. This study examines how magnetic reconnection within X-ray bursts generates self-sustaining vortices in gas disks, a mechanism that could alter disk physics and chemistry by injecting substantial heating and turbulent mixing. A newly identified "stochastic viscous" mechanism is proposed, where the intrinsic viscosity of the disk fluctuates due to the localized heating and altered angular-momentum transport caused by these vortices. This effect is analyzed using X-ray Comptonization and hadronic models, revealing that such stochastic viscosity can induce significant mass accretion variability and alter the observed spectral energy distribution. The research highlights that this mechanism may be a primary driver of outbursts and timing chaos observed in T-Tauri disks and could generate the heating patterns seen in solar-nebula isotope records.

This paper introduces a method for addressing regularized distributionally robust learning in a decentralized framework, specifically accounting for shifts in data distribution. By integrating a Kullback-Leibler regularization term into a robust min-max optimization, this learning task is defined over the probability distribution space. The proposed algorithm, named DR-DSGD, is designed to be solved in a fully decentralized and non-iid environment where the underlying distribution may vary. The approach utilizes an $\epsilon$-shot noise approximation for the shifts in data distribution, updated dynamically through communication across network nodes. Theoretical analysis demonstrates convergence, proving that the algorithm reaches an $\approx$-order optimal robust minimax rate ($\Theta(\sqrt{\epsilon})$) within $O(1/\epsilon)$ iterations to reach this precision level, assuming full connectivity. The method's practical viability is validated by experimental results obtained from MNIST and FashionMNIST datasets.

This paper examines historical computer simulations of the two-dimensional hard-disk model, a theoretical framework developed to explore how particle interactions dictate the physical properties of fluids and granular materials. Despite its simple definition—a collection of discs that cannot overlap due to exclusion—the hard-disk model has driven significant scientific advances for over half a century by posing clear, rigorous challenges. These successful simulations not only confirmed existing models but also inspired the creation of broader simulation methodologies, statistical mechanical theories, and new exacting problems for mathematical investigation, cementing the hard-disk as a cornerstone in computer-aided physics research.

This study presents a general gauge-invariant framework for analyzing photon-assisted electron transport through nanostructures, utilizing tight-binding models that integrate ab initio electron densities and minimally coupled Bloch states. Such models are essential for interpreting current-voltage spectra measured in nanodevices under biased photonic or microwonic irradiation. While gauge invariance is an inherent attribute of dynamical tight-binding models in infinite periodic crystals, achieving this property in finite nanostructures is significantly more complex. We apply our formalism to derive the gauge-invariant time-evolution equation for occupation probabilities within these models, effectively ruling out recently proposed invariant interactions in this context. Additionally, we demonstrate the application of this model to simulate a quantum dot subjected to microwave fields, comparing simulation outcomes against time-resolved experimental data regarding microwave-induced current oscillations.

We examine a specific class of contractible, variationally efficient holographic tensor networks that function as approximate, manifestly defined quantum error-correcting codes capable of yielding states with power-law correlations, addressing a notable gap as most such constructions only produce correlations decaying exponentially. Our approach involves a multi-stage process: initially, a Quantum Extensive Correcting (QEC) block with a linear geometry maps a state exhibiting exponential decay into one featuring power-law characteristics; subsequently, a series of single-layer, three-dimensional Hextatic-Q (HHMERA) blocks connects the two stages. The design of these proposed single-layer operations serves as the foundation for building scalable, multi-layered architectures. Most significantly, while preserving the advantages of explicitness and efficiency, our framework maintains the ability to construct a universal ground state simulator capable of overcoming the short correlation length constraints typically inherent in standard Hextatic-Q models.

A two-state, two-mode computational model is employed to investigate retinal photoisomerization, investigating how steady-state populations in a biophysical environment respond to non-equilibrium conditions and weak thermal and anharmonic couplings. The results indicate that steady-state population levels are governed by specific parameters in a strongly non-intuitive, highly nonlinear, and non-monotonic manner. These findings point to the existence of unexplored new phenomena within nonequilibrium systems. Consequently, this behavior suggests that bio-regulation mechanisms could leverage steep parametric sensitivities for highly efficient sensory functions.

Deep-learning techniques have recently proven effective in numerous domains, including natural language processing and computer vision. To our knowledge, this paper offers the initial exploration of applying such methods to Business Process Model and Enhancement (BPME) tasks, specifically within the contexts of process definition, execution, and fault detection. We evaluate three distinct approaches: Long Short-Term Memory networks, Gated Recurrent Units, and Graph Neural Networks, assessing their efficacy in both process generation (synthesis) and fault detection. Finally, we recommend the proposed Graph-based Convolutional Neural Network as the superior method for these specific applications.

Turkey lies within a highly active seismic zone, exposing it to significant earthquake risks. On October 18, 2020, a magnitude 7.0 tremor struck the city of Izmir in western Turkey, resulting in widespread panic and public confusion regarding potential aftershocks. This study focuses on public tweets related to the disaster to understand their volume, content, and sentiment. By analyzing IZMIR-specific data from Twiiter, we explore how to measure public opinion on social media. The methodology involves web scraping techniques, the use of Python programming, and the application of the VADER sentiment analysis tool for Izmir-centric hashtags. Results indicate that "LALAL" (likely "AFAD") emerged as the most frequent hashtag in discussions. Furthermore, the overall sentiment reflected in the IZMIR-related Twitter data was categorized as mixed, encompassing neutral, negative, and positive classifications.

This study conducts a comprehensive theoretical investigation of light propagation in finite periodic photonic lattices governed by PT-symmetry in both anti-symmetric (anti-PT) and PT-similar regimes. We analytically examine the interplay between bidirectional Perfect Transmittance (PT) and the transition between the PT and anti-PT regimes, which yields non-Hermitian bound states residing in the exceptional points. Furthermore, the paper explores coherent perfect absorption-lasing (CPL) holes within the anti-PT regime, noting that its parameters share exceptional point coordinates with those of the bound states but differ in location relative to the anti-PT zone. We also detail the structural composition of PT and anti-PT bound modes, highlighting their localization at exceptional points within specific lattice sites. The theoretical predictions are corroborated by numerical simulations based on the coupled-mode equations.

We present an investigation into the dynamics of non-equilibrium sparse Boolean networks characterized by self-interactions and self-loops, which are frequently omitted in prior research due to their impact on network dynamics and computational complexity, particularly when nodes influence multiple downstream targets. By employing the specific case of triad connectivity to reveal general principles applicable to hypergraphs, we determine precise conditions governing graph evolution and identify a parameter regime—defined by sparse interconnections and self-interactions—where triad polarity remains locked. This triad-level order is subsequently aggregated to construct a graph-level description that captures the growth or decay of structural motifs, including cliques and stars, within the system. These overarching patterns offer valuable insights into more complex, higher-order Boolean networks and provide a pathway for analyzing the dynamical behaviors of multistate lattice models.

Neural networks employing point clouds have demonstrated significant potential in computer vision, yet they often overfit due to an inability to generalize learned features across different models. To address this, we introduce Transformation Point Clouds (TPC), a novel framework utilizing stochastic smoothing to improve robustness and generalization. Within this framework, a single 3D object is rendered into multiple views, each associated with a random camera transformation to capture diverse perspectives. Using only single-image supervision, the single-view object encoder and transformation-specific smoothing network are trained jointly on this varied point cloud data. Specifically, the stochastic smoothing network learns transformation-specific smoothing functions that map stochastic variations in 3D coordinates to consistent, robust representations, with these functions tied explicitly to each 3D transformation. Experiments on the ShapeOCS and SceneOCS benchmarks confirm our methods outperform state-oftheart approaches, offering superior generalization and view-invariance for novel 3D reconstruction and single-view multi-view rendering tasks.
